records.title: Statue of Nephthys
records.description: Nephthys, whose name means Mistress of the House, was an important figure in ancient Egyptian funerary beliefs. She and her sister Isis mourned their brother Osiris and became archetypal mourners for the dead. This figure is shown kneeling in the standard mourning position. Nephthys and Isis were often depicted at either end of a coffin or sarcophagus. The statue is most likely connected with this funerary context.
records.sourceTitle: Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities, Egypt

records.title: Osiris Statuette
records.description: Osiris was the god of vegetation and the underworld and was associated with the weighing of the heart. Statuettes of Osiris were made to be placed in tombs. His death, mummification and transition to the afterlife were central to funerary beliefs.
records.sourceTitle: Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities, Egypt

records.title: A wooden model of a Funerary boat
records.description: Boats were used to transport the mummy to the cemetery on the western bank of the Nile. The coffin was accompanied by relatives and funerary priests, including two women representing Isis and Nephthys.
records.sourceTitle: Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities, Egypt

records.title: The Mummy of Masaharti
records.description: Masaharti was a general of the army and high priest of Amun at Thebes, and son of King Pinedjem I. His mummy was found in the royal cache at Deir el-Bahri in 1881. It dates to the 21st Dynasty; the face was painted with red ochre and a gold finger cap remains on the middle finger of the right hand.
records.sourceTitle: Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities, Egypt

records.title: Statue and mummy of a cat
records.description: The object combines a statue and mummy of a cat, a sacred animal of the goddess Bastet. The Ministry catalogue notes the importance of Bastet's cult in the Late Period, especially at Tell Basta (Zagazig), and identifies the statue wood as sycamore.
records.sourceTitle: Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities, Egypt

records.title: Narmer Palette
records.description: The Narmer Palette contains some of the earliest hieroglyphic inscriptions. It is thought to depict the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt under King Narmer. It shows the king wearing the Red Crown and the White Crown, and includes intertwined serpopards. The Ministry catalogue dates it to the Early Dynastic Period, 1st Dynasty, around 3100 BC; its medium is green schist and its provenance is Hierakonpolis.
records.period: Early Dynastic Period, 1st Dynasty, reign of Narmer, c. 3100 BC
records.sourceTitle: Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities, Egypt

records.title: Statue of Mentuhotep II (Nebhepetre)
records.description: The seated painted sandstone statue represents King Nebhepetre Mentuhotep II (Mentuhotep II), the ruler who reunified Upper and Lower Egypt and established the Middle Kingdom after the First Intermediate Period. He wears the Red Crown of Lower Egypt and the close-fitting jubilee garment associated with the Sed festival. His crossed arms and black-painted skin associate him with Osiris and ideas of death, fertility, and resurrection. The statue was discovered by Howard Carter in 1900 inside a subterranean chamber (Bab el-Hosan) in the king's mortuary complex at Deir el-Bahari. The official Egyptian Museum Cairo record lists it in Gallery 26 on the Ground Floor.
records.period: Middle Kingdom, 11th Dynasty, reign of Nebhepetre Mentuhotep II (c. 2055–2004 BC)
records.location: The Egyptian Museum, Cairo, Gallery 26, Ground Floor
records.sourceTitle: Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities, Egypt
